label.INDTRUSTASMB: Percentage who tend to trust the NI Assembly, or trust it a great deal

result.label: Indicator - Trust in the NI Assembly
note:
[b]Trust in the NI Assembly[/b]

[b]How do we measure this?[/b] 
Percentage of the population aged 16+ who said they tend to trust the Northern Ireland Assembly, or trust it a great deal. For this indicator a higher figure is better.

[b]Source[/b] 
Public Awareness of and Trust in Official Statistics 
[url=https://www.nisra.gov.uk/statistics/government/public-awareness-and-confidence-trust-official-statistics-pcos]https://www.nisra.gov.uk/statistics/government/public-awareness-and-confidence-trust-official-statistics-pcos[/url] 

[b]Impact of Covid-19[/b] 
In 2020, the data collection ran for an additional three months (October 2020 to March 2021) to achieve the required sample size. Data collection also changed from face-to-face to telephone interviewing for 2020 and 2021, with both data collection modes used from 2022. 

[b]Further Information[/b] 
1. Data for 2025 is currently available at Northern Ireland level only. Subpopulation data for this indicator is expected to be available by autumn 2026.
2. In 2019 and 2023, respondents were asked whether they trusted elected bodies, such as the NI Assembly or the UK Parliament as the NI Assembly was suspended at this time.
3. The Public Awareness and Trust in Official Statistics survey only ran in ‘even’ years prior to 2019. Results are not available for 2018, due to an irreparable issue with the source data.
4. The percentages for this indicator are estimated based on a sample of the population and so will have some uncertainty. As the sample size increases, the uncertainty decreases. When calculating the bounds for ‘improving’ and ‘worsening’ in the PfG indicator dashboard the sample sizes for the latest available year (2025) and the comparison year (2021) have been used. This means that we are 95% confident that the trend is ‘worsening’ or ‘improving’ compared to 2021 if the value for 2025 falls in these regions.
5. You can view and download confidence intervals on the [url=product/TINIA]NISRA Data Portal[/url].

[b]Sex[/b] 
6. There was no significant difference between the percentage of males and females who trusted the NI Assembly in any year in the time series. Further information on how to interpret the survey estimates and confidence intervals for the estimated percentages are available in the Trust in the NI Assembly data tables, 2024: [url=https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024]https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024[/url] 

[b]Age[/b] 
7. In 2022 and 2024, those aged 75 and over were significantly more likely to trust the NI Assembly than those aged 35 to 44, 45 to 54 and 55 to 64; and in 2019 and 2020 this age group were significantly more likely to trust the NI Assembly/Elected bodies than those aged 25 to 44, 35 to 54 and 55 to 64. In 2019 and 2021, those aged 25 to 34 were significantly less likely to trust the NI Assembly/Elected bodies than those aged 45 to 54, 55 to 64 and 75 and over (in 2019), and those aged 35 to 44, 45 to 54 and 75 and over (in 2021). Further information on how to interpret the survey estimates, additional analysis and confidence intervals for the estimates are available in the Trust in the NI Assembly data tables, 2024: [url=https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024]https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024[/url] 
8. Sample sizes for those aged 16 to 24 were too small to produce reliable estimates (less than 100 respondents).

[b]Marital status[/b] 
9. In 2021 and 2023, individuals with a marital status of other (separated, divorced/dissolved or widowed) were significantly less likely to trust the NI Assembly/Elected bodies than those who were married or in a civil partnership, and in 2014 and 2021, those with a marital status of other (separated, divorced/dissolved or widowed) were significantly less likely to trust the NI Assembly than those who were single. All other differences are not significant. Further information on how to interpret the survey estimates and confidence intervals for the estimated percentages are available in Trust in the NI Assembly data tables, 2024: [url=https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024]https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024[/url] 
10. ‘Other’ includes those with a marital status of: Separated (but still legally married or still legally in a civil partnership), Divorced or formerly in a civil partnership which is now legally dissolved, Widowed or surviving member of a legally registered civil partnership. 

[b]Religion[/b] 
11. In 2020, Catholics and those from ‘Protestant and other Christian religions’ were significantly more likely to trust the NI Assembly than those from ‘Other religions and no religion’. In 2023, those from ‘Protestant and other Christian religions’ were significantly more likely to trust Elected bodies than Catholics. All other differences are not significant. Further information on how to interpret the survey estimates and confidence intervals for the estimated percentages are available in Trust in the NI Assembly data tables, 2024: [url=https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024]https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024[/url] 
12. The category ‘Protestant’ includes those from ‘Protestant and other Christian religions’. 
13. ‘no religion’ only includes those individuals who stated that they had no religion. Respondents who did not answer the question were not included in the analysis. 
14. Data is provided from the first year available (2019).

[b]Dependants[/b] 
15. In 2019, those with dependants were significantly less likely to trust Elected bodies than those without dependants. All other differences are not significant. Further information on how to interpret the survey estimates and confidence intervals for the estimated percentages are available in Trust in the NI Assembly data tables, 2024: [url=https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024]https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024[/url] 
16. ‘With dependants (overall)’ includes individuals who have responsibility for the care of a child, a person with a disability and/or a dependant elderly person. 

[b]Disability[/b] 
17. In 2022, 2023 and 2024, individuals with a disability were significantly less likely to trust the NI Assembly/Elected bodies than those without a disability. All other differences are not significant. Further information on how to interpret the survey estimates and confidence intervals for the estimated percentages are available in Trust in the NI Assembly data tables, 2024: [url=https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024]https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024[/url]
18. Individuals are defined as having a disability if they have any physical or mental health conditions or illnesses lasting or expected to last for 12 months or more, and the condition(s) or illness(es) reduce their ability to carry out day to day activities.
19. Information on disability was not collected in 2020. 

[b]Ethnic group[/b] 
20. ‘Other’ includes: Irish Traveller; White and Black Caribbean; White and Black African; White and Asian; Any other Mixed/Multiple ethnic background; Indian; Pakistani; Bangladeshi; Chinese; Any other Asian background; African; Caribbean; Any other Black/African/Caribbean background; Arab; Any other ethnic group. 
21. Estimates are only available for 'White' as sample sizes were too small to produce reliable estimates for 'Other’ ethnic group (less than 100 respondents). Further information on how to interpret the survey estimates, additional analysis and confidence intervals for the estimates are available in the Trust in the NI Assembly data tables, 2024: [url=https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024]https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024[/url] 

[b]Sexual orientation[/b] 
22. Respondents were presented with four options (Heterosexual or straight; Gay or Lesbian; Bisexual; Other) and asked to 'select the option which best describes how you think of yourself'.
23. Estimates were only available for 'Heterosexual or straight' as sample sizes were too small to produce reliable estimates for 'Gay, lesbian, bisexual and other' (less than 100 respondents). Further information on how to interpret the survey estimates, additional analysis and confidence intervals for the estimates are available in the Trust in the NI Assembly data tables, 2024: [url=https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024]https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024[/url] 
24. Sexual orientation data is available for all years except 2020 and 2021.

[b]Deprivation[/b] 
25. In 2021, individuals living in the most deprived areas in Northern Ireland (Quintile 1) were significantly less likely to trust the NI Assembly than those living in Quintiles 2, 3 or 5, and in 2023 they were significantly less likely to trust Elected bodies than those living in Quintiles 2, 4 and 5. Further information on how to interpret the survey estimates, additional analysis and confidence intervals for the estimates are available in the Trust in the NI Assembly data tables, 2024: [url=https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024]https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024[/url] 
26. Respondents have been assigned to a deprivation quintile based on the area in which they live. Small areas in Northern Ireland are ranked using the 2017 NI Multiple Deprivation Measure. Quintile 1 represents the 20% most deprived areas, and Quintile 5 represents the 20% least deprived areas. More information on the NI Multiple Deprivation Measures can be found here: [url=https://www.nisra.gov.uk/statistics/deprivation/northern-ireland-multiple-deprivation-measure-2017-nimdm2017]https://www.nisra.gov.uk/statistics/deprivation/northern-ireland-multiple-deprivation-measure-2017-nimdm2017[/url] 
27. Data is provided from the first year available (2019).

[b]Urban Rural[/b] 
28. In 2020 and 2024, individuals living in rural areas were significantly more likely to trust the NI Assembly than those living in urban areas. All other differences are not significant. Further information on how to interpret the survey estimates and confidence intervals for the estimated percentages are available in Trust in the NI Assembly data tables, 2024: [url=https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024]https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/pfg-trust-in-the-media-and-trust-in-the-NI-assembly-2024[/url] 
29. Respondents have been categorised as living in an urban or rural area based on the 2015 (settlement based) urban rural classification. More information on urban rural classifications can be found here: [url=https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/urban-rural-geography-documents-2015]https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/urban-rural-geography-documents-2015[/url]
30. Data is provided from the first year available (2019).
